extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry, drama, and literary criticism (writers and critics applying Aristotelian principles)
extracted.subtask_description: Applying Aristotle's principles from the Poetics to evaluate or compose poetry and drama — focusing on poetic truth, probability, unity, and the admissibility of the marvelous, chance, and irrational elements. Useful for poets, dramatists, and critics shaping plots and character motives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth vs factual truth
rubrics_metrics.description: The truth of poetry is essentially different from the truth of fact; poetry may depict things that never happened and never will, yet be 'more true, poetically speaking' than daily occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet should purify legendary or historical material from the accidental, trivial and irrelevant — 'to free it from the dross which always mingles with empirical reality' — idealising experience so that imaginative truth is revealed rather than mere reportage. Poetry presents permanent and eternal facts, free from elements of unreason that disturb comprehension of real events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Probable impossibilities are to be preferred to improbable possibilities.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Through artistic treatment the impossible may appear natural and inevitable; vivid narrative, minuteness of detail, and internal consistency can make incredible events seem as they would have happened if the poetic premises were real (examples: Homer's magic ship, Odysseus' landing). The poet aims to make the impossible 'πιθανά' (probable) by preserving inner consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permission to 'tell lies skilfully' (poetic fiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet has the privilege, even the duty, 'ψευδῆ λέγειν ὡς δεῖ' — to tell lies skilfully: he must learn the true art of fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet may create primary assumptions (the poetic data) and build a world from them, carrying the audience along so long as the poet does not 'dash us against the prosaic ground of fact.' The secret lies in starting from poetic presuppositions and maintaining the natural sequence of incident and motive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish material impossibility from moral improbability (moral improbability is graver)
rubrics_metrics.description: Material impossibilities (physical anomalies) can often be reconciled by imaginative acceptance, but moral improbabilities — actions motiveless or incompatible with human character — are more serious and tend to be artistic defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While material improbability can be absorbed if the chain of cause and effect within the fiction remains unbroken, moral improbability violates the laws of conduct and character and resists imaginative surrender. Avoid motiveless acts or actions contrary to a character's established nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrational elements (ἄλογα) must be justified and are riskier than mere impossibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that offend reason (ἄλογα) are greater stumbling-blocks for the poetic sense than material impossibilities and need special justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The irrational tends to provoke the logical faculty; it may be admitted chiefly where it heightens wonder and admiration (an effect proper to epic), and even then only under strict limitations. The poet should disguise or integrate such elements so they appear reasonable within the work's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supernatural and traditional legend admissible when coherent with cultural belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Marvellous or supernatural facts may be proper material for poetry when they are enshrined in popular legend or coherent national belief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If myths or legends have been worked into a people's imagination and express underlying sentiments, they may be used because they 'are not among the ἄλογα of poetry.' The poet can often efface lines between natural and supernatural and incorporate both into a single rational-imaginative order — but only when the tradition gives them a coherent shape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stricter limits on irrationality in drama than in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle regards the irrational (whether supernatural or motiveless human activity) as less admissible in dramatic than in epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama, being a representation of human action whose mainspring is motive, should exclude motiveless or causeless elements from the action itself; if such elements are used they should serve as part of the plot's antecedents (not occur within the represented action) and must be made to look at least somewhat plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of chance/accident unless art makes it appear designed
rubrics_metrics.description: Chance (τὸ συμβεβηκός) is essentially the negation of art — disorder, absence of design — and is generally excluded by the law of the probable or the necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art seeks ideal unity and design; accidental anomalies should not be introduced simply as 'strange chances.' Chance may be admitted only where the poet's skill imparts an appearance of design, or where chance's effects can be shown to fit the work's internal logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy and tragedy should be framed on probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Even comedy, like tragedy, should be 'framed on lines of probability' rather than representing a world of gratuitous chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although comic plots may have a looser connexion of incidents than tragedy and be less rigorously bound by necessity, their incidents are still expected to follow probable sequences and not rest on mere accident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and wholeness: a plot must be a single, complete action
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot must, as in a tragedy, be dramatically constructed as 'a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poetic work should exhibit organic unity: parts must be inwardly connected and arranged in a necessary order so the whole resembles a living organism. Size and proportion matter: too small a work shows only unity, too large shows only parts; the ideal balances plurality and unity to produce the proper pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form dominates matter; art imposes form on chosen material
rubrics_metrics.description: In art the matter depends on the artist's choice; form is imposed on matter and is primary for the work's life and unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The artist imparts a form that gives the semblance of life; the poetic form must determine appropriate quantity, proportion, and relation of parts to the whole. The creator must choose matter that serves the imposed form and maintain proportion and symmetry throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal through the particular (poetry nearer to philosophy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry is 'more philosophical and a higher thing than history' because it expresses the universal (τὰ καθόλου) through particularised, sensuous imagery; it approaches the universal and is nearer to philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should aim to present universal truths via concrete, living embodiments (organismic wholes). It is not abstract philosophy but conjoins universal import with sensory detail — offering a manifestation of causes through imagistic representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended compositional method: outline the general idea, then add detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle advises setting forth the plot in its general idea (ἐκτίθεσθαι καθόλου), abstracting accidental features of time, place, and persons, and afterwards filling it in with detail, incident, and proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as a practical order of composition (whether drawing from legend or invention). The text notes the value may be questioned as practical advice, but distinguishes this procedural 'καθόλου' (broad outline) from the philosophical 'καθόλου' (the universal truth poetry conveys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the lawless, the fantastic, and wanton violation of nature's principles
rubrics_metrics.description: While the poet may transcend nature, he 'must not contradict her; he must not be disobedient to her habits and principles' — avoiding the lawless, fantastic, and impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic transcendence is permitted only so far as it does not 'wantonly violate the laws which make the real world rational.' The poet recreates the actual but must avoid anomalies of experience that amount to artistic defects unless convincingly integrated into the poem's internal necessity.
